idiom_name: templated forwarding wrapper over the target (pro::proxy / std::function style)
implementation_notes: Standard C++ cannot define a class at run time: static reflection (P2996) is compile-time only and injected declarations cannot come from runtime state, so the practical proxy is generated by templates. A forwarding wrapper stores the target and implements each interface member by delegating, while type-erasure facilities (std::function, the proposed pro::proxy facade) hold an arbitrary implementation behind one call surface when the concrete type must not leak. The classic form is justified only when the interface set is genuinely unknown to the compiler - then libffi closures or an interpreter host are needed.
pitfalls: A hand-written forwarder rots: adding a virtual member to the interface still compiles, and calls through the base then skip the proxy entirely.
Value semantics are hostile to proxies: the interface reference held by the wrapper must outlive it, and copying a proxied value slices the target instead of the wrapper.
Type-erasure wrappers hide ownership: accept pointers or references at the boundary deliberately, or the wrapper outlives what it forwards to.

variants.name: runtime-generated trampolines via libffi
variants.idiom_name: ffi_closure_alloc/ffi_prep_closure_loc wrapped in a template closure factory
variants.implementation_notes: When the method set is discovered at run time (plugin ABI, foreign runtime), libffi closures can fabricate callable entries, and a small template wrapper turns a member function plus object pointer into the C function the trampoline calls. It is the only route to runtime proxy entries that does not depend on a bytecode library, and it trades type safety for that reach.
pitfalls: Struct-by-value arguments and non-trivial return types need correctly built ffi_type descriptors; a wrong descriptor corrupts the stack instead of raising an error.
Generated entries sit outside the type system: the compiler cannot check that the trampoline signature matches the interface it stands in for.

variants.name: C++26 static reflection-generated proxy class
variants.idiom_name: std::meta reflection plus injected class members (P2996, P3157 proxy classes)
variants.implementation_notes: C++26 reflection turns the hand-written forwarder into a generated one at compile time: reflect the interface, walk its member functions, and inject a class whose members delegate - the 'proxy class and instrumented class' use case argued in P3157. That removes the per-method boilerplate without introducing runtime code generation, and is the direction C++ proxy code should take once toolchains ship it.
pitfalls: Injected declarations are compile-time constructs: a proxy for an interface discovered at run time remains impossible, and toolchain conformance is still new.
Generated members can capture intent wrongly (const, noexcept, ref-qualifiers) unless the forwarding rules are derived from the reflected signature instead of written by hand.
